extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Milton / literary scholars interested in prose rhetoric and the history of the press
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and critical criteria for assessing Milton's prose (Areopagitica and related works), comparing it with classical models (Isokrates) and situating it in the political/contextual history of press licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek exemplar influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's reading-speech/prose works are modeled on Greek examples (Isokrates in prose; Greek tragic form for Samson Agonistes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the work for explicit classical models, Greek names/mottos, structural echoes (e.g., Areopagitica named after Isokrates' Areopagitic discourse), and how Greek forms inform purpose and arrangement. The page notes Milton 'found Greek example' and repeatedly compares his aims and methods with Isokrates and Greek tragic poets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience choice — learned vs popular
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton deliberately targeted an 'elegant and learned reader' rather than popular approval ('fit audience, though few'; 'to be heard only ... by the elegant and learned reader').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the writing presumes specialist knowledge, classical references, and complexity that limits broad accessibility. Consider intentional appeals to a select, learned readership as a rhetorical and ethical choice rather than a flaw.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polish and prolonged composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Exemplary rhetorical works are the product of long, careful composition and polishing (Isokrates reportedly spent ten to fifteen years on his Panegyric Oration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge prose on evidence of careful revision, structural symmetry, and sustained craftsmanship. The text treats extended labor in composition as a positive standard of excellence ('The immense care he bestowed... may be inferred from the statement that he was engaged for a period of ten, and, according to others, of fifteen years').

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuity and refined clarity (Isokrates ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Isokrates' prose is praised as 'exquisitely refined and clear' — 'the marble is smoothed to the utmost' — perspicuous even if 'not so very much' in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity, economy, and refinement of expression: whether sentences are lucid, well-polished, and avoid unnecessary obscurity. Note trade-offs: perspicuity may favor surface clarity over depth ('The water is pellucid, but then it is not deep').

rubrics_metrics.name: Profound substance and expansive eloquence (Milton ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's prose is characterized by an abundance of thought and knowledge, with 'thoughts rush[ing] upon him in a throng' and an eloquence that can 'wellnigh overmaster' him; his sentences possess 'stately majesty.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work's intellectual ambition and depth: richness of learning, moral/philosophical weight, and energetic rhetorical force. Allow that such profundity may produce very long, ornate periods and occasional obscurity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periodic sentence structure and antithesis
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark is the old 'periodic' style: antithetical and expanded sentences, marshalling clauses in successive groups; this can produce grandeur but also risk of obscurity in English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging style, examine use of long periodic sentences, antithesis, and elaborate grouping of clauses. Consider language-specific effects: Greek's inflections and linking particles can sustain complexity without obscurity, but in English periodicity may 'lead to obscurity' and require 'great care' from the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form suitability — choosing prose or metre
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of form matters: for Milton 'metre was absolutely necessary' for full expression of his poetic genius; prose could feel 'maimed' or 'left hand' compared to poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the chosen medium (prose vs verse) fits the author's expressive needs. Consider whether constraints of a form (e.g., metre) provide productive restraint or whether prose better serves argumentative clarity and political address.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical parallels and rhetorical exempla
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton uses parallels (e.g., comparing contemporary figures/events with Isokrates' times) and classical exempla to justify names, aims, and political positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how effectively classical analogies are used to illuminate, persuade, or legitimize arguments. Check fitness of parallels and whether they clarify or obscure the contemporary argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection of oratory to politics — persuasive public purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: A valued dimension is rhetoric explicitly linked to political ends: Isokrates 'connecting oratory and politics' and Milton addressing Parliament from private house; rhetorical pieces aim to persuade on political reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the work's rhetorical tactics for political persuasion: clarity of audience (e.g., parliament), appropriateness of appeals, and alignment between form/content and political objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of censorship and political risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers had to reckon with licensers and possible expurgation (examples: Paradise Lost lines examined by licenser; History of Britain suffered excisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing or assessing political prose, consider topical risk: how provocative lines might attract censorship, whether the author adapts language to avoid suppression, and how expurgation affects integrity. Historical context of press regulation (Ordinances, Act of 1662, lapsed 1694) is relevant to evaluating rhetorical choices.
